title: Kotanko family seeks answers in man's death
subtitle: `Cone of silence' descends on gunsmith's death
article: The family of Rodger Kotanko is determined to keep his name in the public eye while the Special Investigations Unit probes the circumstances of his death Nov. 3 during an interaction with members of the Toronto Police Service.

The family gathered in front of Kotanko's home on Port Ryerse Road west of Port Dover Thursday for a news conference regarding his death. Speaking on their behalf was Simcoe lawyer Michael Smitiuch, a specialist in personal injury law.
"We're not announcing a lawsuit," Smitiuch said. "We're in the dark like you are.
"But this does cry of negligence. It seems the planning of this was botched, as was the raid."

Members of the Toronto Police Service executed a search warrant at Kotanko's home around noon Nov. 3. Kotanko, 70, was a licensed gunsmith who occasionally did work for members of the Norfolk OPP, which was not involved in this operation.
Smitiuch confirmed Kotanko was shot four times inside his workshop next to his home. Kotanko was with a "customer," Smitiuch said, with the shots coming from outside the building.

"A cone of silence" has descended over the matter since the SIU invoked its mandate, Smitiuch said. Answers to even basic questions, he said, are not forthcoming. Smitiuch shared questions he and the Kotanko family want answers to. These include:

A reporter brought to Smitiuch's attention that the police action at Kotanko's home coincided with the execution of 15 search warrants across south-central Ontario as part of Project Gainsborough, also on Nov. 3. Project Gainsborough resulted in the seizure of a large amount of contraband marijuana and cannabis products among other illegal items. Among the many police forces participating in Project Gainsborough was the Toronto Police Service.

Two of the warrants executed were in Norfolk County according to the Ontario Provincial Police, although the locations were not disclosed. Smitiuch said "that doesn't sound like a coincidence" before adding it to his list of unanswered questions surrounding events at Kotanko's home.
Smitiuch said Kotanko did not know the identity of the "customer" and that he had arranged to meet the gunsmith the night before in a phone call at 10 p.m.
An investigation into the customer's identity might begin by reviewing Kotanko's phone logs, Smitiuch said.

However, that's not possible at the moment because police seized Kotanko's phone and have not returned it. Toronto police have also not provided the family with a manifest of property seized at the scene, raising questions about what the SIU is seeing as part of its investigation.

Also speaking at the conference was Kotanko's sister Suzanne Kantor. Kantor said her brother was careful to protect his gunsmith licence, turning down potential customers if he suspected the job was outside the rules.
"That's why we're really struggling as to how they could just come in here and do something like this," she said. "He was a teddy bear. He was harmless. Right now we're just baffled.
"It's scary to think they could do to anybody what they did to my brother and not provide any answers. That is totally wrong."

Kotanko's brother Jeff has started a campaign encouraging interested citizens to tie a black ribbon to the antenna of their vehicle as a reminder of what happened Nov. 3. That, Kotanko said, is another way of keeping this incident in the public eye while the SIU does its work.
"One time, he told me he'd probably die sitting at his bench," Jeff Kotanko said. "But I don't think he ever thought he'd be gunned down while sitting at his bench by a police task force.
"It's really stupid - that's what it is."

In an update Thursday afternoon, the SIU reported that one "subject official" is under investigation while seven "witness officials" have been designated. Five witness officials have been interviewed, the SIU says, as have two civilian witnesses.

The SIU added that one police-issued firearm has been secured and sent to the Centre for Forensic Sciences for analysis. A post mortem was conducted on Kotanko Nov. 4 - the day after the shooting - with the SIU awaiting the results.
"Mr. Kotanko's next-of-kin are engaged in the SIU's Affected Persons Program, which includes support services," SIU spokesperson Kristy Denette said.
